q: Which fracture pattern is MOST consistent with non-accidental injury (NAI) rather than a single accidental event?
o: Isolated greenstick fracture of the distal radius in a 6-month-old puppy
Bilateral carpal fractures in a 10-year-old dog with nutritional secondary hyperparathyroidism
Single transverse fracture of the femur with a consistent history of being hit by a car
Multiple fractures in different anatomical regions, each in a different stage of healing
e: Multiple fractures in different stages of healing in different body regions indicate injuries occurring at multiple points in time — this cannot be explained by a single event and is the hallmark radiographic finding of NAI. Greenstick fractures are typical accidental fractures in young animals. A single femur fracture with a consistent history is not suspicious in isolation. Metabolic bone disease can produce multiple fractures but the history and blood work would support this diagnosis.

q: Subconjunctival and scleral hemorrhages in a cat without external facial trauma are MOST consistent with:
o: Anterior uveitis secondary to FIP
Sudden increase in intracranial or intrathoracic pressure from shaking or choking
Hypertensive retinopathy from chronic kidney disease
Primary coagulopathy causing spontaneous hemorrhage
e: Subconjunctival and scleral hemorrhages without external facial trauma are classic findings in shaken or choked animals. The sudden rise in intracranial/intrathoracic pressure forces blood through conjunctival and scleral vessels. This is a well-recognised NAI finding in both veterinary and human forensic medicine. While hypertension and coagulopathy are differentials, the NAI context makes shaking/choking the leading consideration.

q: A dog presents with hemoabdomen, pale mucous membranes, and tachycardia. On abdominal radiographs there is free fluid and the diaphragm is not visible as a distinct line. The MOST likely injury consistent with blunt NAI is:
o: Ruptured spleen or liver AND diaphragmatic hernia from high-energy abdominal compression
Bile peritonitis from a ruptured common bile duct
Ruptured urinary bladder from urethral obstruction
Splenic torsion with concurrent ascites from hypoproteinaemia
e: High-energy blunt abdominal compression (stomping, kicking) can simultaneously rupture abdominal organs causing hemoabdomen and tear the diaphragm causing a diaphragmatic hernia. The loss of a distinct diaphragmatic line on radiograph is a key indicator of diaphragmatic hernia. Both findings together in the NAI context point to a single high-energy compressive event.

q: Which animal best fits the ASPCA NAI high-risk animal profile?
o: 6-year-old spayed female Golden retriever, annual wellness exam, no injuries
8-year-old spayed female Labrador retriever, calm, friendly with owner
10-month-old intact male mixed-breed dog, 12 lbs (5.4 kg), cowers and urinates when the owner approaches
4-year-old neutered male domestic shorthair cat, indoor only, normal physical exam
e: This dog hits multiple ASPCA NAI risk factors: age <2 years, intact male, mixed breed, small (<15 lbs (6.8 kg)), and showing fearful behaviour specifically toward the caretaker (cowering and urinating on approach). No single factor confirms NAI, but the combination of multiple risk factors in this animal warrants heightened vigilance.

q: An owner brings in a dog with a femur fracture. They state the dog "fell off the couch yesterday." On exam you also note a 3-week-old healing rib fracture and fresh bruising on the dorsal thorax. Which of the following best describes your obligation?
o: Accept the history; couch falls can cause femur fractures in small dogs
Document all findings objectively, treat the animal, and report to animal control or law enforcement
Withhold treatment until law enforcement arrives and takes a statement from the owner
Confront the owner directly and demand an explanation for the rib fracture before treating
e: Multiple fractures in different healing stages with fresh bruising are incompatible with the stated mechanism. Document objectively ("owner stated animal fell from a couch; physical examination reveals a femur fracture, a 3-week-old healing rib fracture, and fresh dorsal thoracic bruising inconsistent with the stated history"). Treat the animal's injuries and report to animal control. Do not withhold emergency care, and do not confront the owner — this can compromise safety and evidence.

q: When performing a full-body radiographic survey on a NAI suspect, which of the following is the MOST important reason for including the skull?
o: Skull radiographs are required by law in cruelty cases
Skull fractures may be occult (not apparent externally) and require significant force — their detection strengthens the NAI diagnosis
Dental radiographs are more sensitive and replace the need for skull films
Skull radiographs identify the breed of the animal for documentation
e: Skull fractures require substantial force and are inconsistent with most accidental injuries described by owners. They can be completely occult on external examination — no external scalp/fur injury. Including the skull in a full-body survey detects occult fractures that strengthen the forensic case. The skull views should include lateral, DV, and oblique projections to maximise fracture detection.

q: Damage to the claws or nail beds of a cat presented as a cruelty case is MOST suggestive of:
o: Dragging, restraint, or direct trauma to the feet consistent with NAI
Onychomycosis from a chronic fungal infection
Self-mutilation secondary to obsessive-compulsive disorder
Nutritional deficiency causing brittle nails
e: Nail bed avulsions, fractured claws, or burns of the claw tips are recognised NAI findings, associated with dragging (claws breaking as the animal is dragged across a surface), restraint (the animal clawing against a surface while restrained), or direct application of heat. Preserve the broken nail material as physical evidence — clip into a sealed, labelled envelope.

q: An owner who brings their dog to a different veterinary clinic each visit and uses a different surname each time is exhibiting which NAI caretaker risk factor?
o: Financial difficulty making it necessary to seek the cheapest available clinic
A requirement for multiple opinions before agreeing to treatment
"Practice shopping" — seeking care from multiple providers to prevent detection of a pattern of repeated injuries
Dissatisfaction with veterinary care quality, a common and benign behaviour
e: Using multiple practices with name discrepancies is a recognised NAI caretaker risk factor, consistent with deliberate "practice shopping" to prevent any single clinic from accumulating a record of repeated injuries. This pattern should be documented. Clinicians who encounter such a pattern should check whether the animal has a microchip that might be registered under previous visits at other practices.

q: In what investigative context is the microwave radiation injury in this kitten most relevant?
o: Genetic disease screening
Vaccine reaction surveillance
Non-accidental injury and maltreatment investigation
Routine nutritional assessment
e: Listed keywords (forensics, maltreatment, microwave radiation, burn management) tie the case to non-accidental injury investigation.

q: A case report of microwave radiation injuries in a 7-week-old kitten emphasizes which clinical skill for shelter and forensic veterinarians?
o: Managing nutritional deficiencies
Performing orthopedic surgery
Interpreting echocardiograms
Recognizing and documenting distinctive thermal burn patterns
e: The case highlights recognizing, documenting, and managing the distinctive burn pattern of microwave radiation injury, a key skill for forensic and shelter veterinarians investigating non-accidental injury.

Accidental death
A euthanasia error
Killing multiple animals
e: Overkilling denotes unusually massive injuries beyond those needed to kill the victim.

q: In a forensic veterinary case report of an 'overkilling' incident involving a dog found with rope restraints in southern Italy, the two concurrent lethal mechanisms confirmed at autopsy were:
o: Drowning and burns
Starvation and dehydration
Gunshot and electrocution
Strangulation and poisoning
e: Strangulation lesions were confirmed histologically, and toxicological testing confirmed concurrent poisoning — demonstrating lethal force far exceeding what was necessary to cause death.

q: In a forensic veterinary overkilling case involving both strangulation and poisoning in a dog, the workup that revealed both concurrent lethal mechanisms comprised:
o: Combined radiography, autopsy, histology, and toxicology
Behavioral testing
A single gross exam
Owner interview alone
e: Full-body radiography, gross autopsy, histopathology, and toxicology together exposed the dual lethal mechanisms in this overkilling case.
